title: Erasmus Mundus Without IELTS: What Consortia Really Accept in 2027
seoTitle: Erasmus Mundus Without IELTS 2027: MOI Rules & Alternatives
seoDescription: Can you apply to Erasmus Mundus without IELTS? How consortium English requirements actually work, when MOI letters work, and which alternatives are accepted in 2027.
intro: There is no single Erasmus Mundus IELTS rule — each consortium sets its own. Here is what EMJM programmes actually accept, when MOI letters work, and how to ask.
description: How Erasmus Mundus English requirements really work, and when you can apply without IELTS using an MOI letter.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: How Erasmus Mundus English requirements really work — and when you can apply without IELTS using an MOI letter.
content:
Search "Erasmus Mundus without IELTS" and you will find hundreds of confident answers, most of them wrong in the same way: Erasmus Mundus is not one programme with one rule. It is a brand attached to roughly ninety separate consortia, and each consortium writes its own English requirement into its own call. There is no Erasmus+ regulation that mandates IELTS — and equally, no blanket waiver. Whether you can apply without IELTS depends entirely on the consortium you target.

What consortia actually ask for

The modal requirement across EMJM calls is IELTS Academic 6.5, with competitive programmes in journalism, public policy and health asking 7.0, and engineering consortia sometimes accepting 6.0. Where scores sit below 6.5, expect band minimums around 6.0. None of this is centrally published — you verify it in the specific call documents of the specific programme, which is exactly what each card in our database links to.

The good news is what consortia accept as evidence is broader than IELTS. The table below summarises how alternatives are treated in practice — not as official policy, but as the pattern across current calls.

What you can show insteadHow consortia treat it
Medium of Instruction (MOI) letterSome consortia accept a letter confirming your degree was taught in English; others refuse it outright. Always ask in writing before relying on it.
TOEFL iBTAccepted nearly everywhere IELTS is; typical floor 90-100 when IELTS 6.5 is asked.
PTE AcademicGrowing acceptance; common floor 59-65.
Duolingo English TestAccepted by a minority of consortia, mostly post-Covid era; treat as a fallback, not a plan.
Cambridge C1/C2Widely accepted at C1 Advanced or better.
A degree from a majority-English countryAlmost universally accepted as an exemption when applicable.

The MOI route, done properly

A Medium of Instruction letter — issued by your university, confirming your degree was taught and examined in English — is the closest thing to a genuine "without IELTS" path, and it works more often than applicants expect. But it is never automatic. The reliable sequence looks like this:

  • Email the consortium before applying. One short question — "will an MOI letter from [university] satisfy the English requirement for the 2027 round?" — gets a written answer you can attach to your file.
  • Get the letter in English, on letterhead, signed. Generic templates translated later create doubt; a clean letter removes it.
  • Ask whether conditional offers exist. Some consortia offer admission with a condition of English proof later — enough time for one IELTS sitting if the waiver is refused.

Keep expectations calibrated: a consortium that states "IELTS 6.5 or equivalent, MOI not accepted" in its call will not bend at interview stage. Spend that energy on the dozens of programmes where the answer is yes or maybe.

The timing question: when to book a test anyway

Even applicants pursuing the no-IELTS route should decide on a test date by mid-November. The arithmetic is simple: if you are applying to three or more consortia, the odds that at least one hard-requires IELTS are high, and winter test slots in most countries sell out weeks ahead. A computer-delivered IELTS Academic costs roughly €200-250, returns results in three to five days, and stays valid for two years — long enough to cover this cycle and a re-application next year. Treat one sitting as insurance for the whole application season: if every consortium on your list accepts an MOI letter, you have lost nothing; if one does not, you are ready while others are on waiting lists.

Band minimums deserve a second look as well. A 6.5 overall with a 5.5 in writing fails more calls than it passes — many consortia specify a floor in each band, typically 6.0. When you read a card’s English line, read the small print under it before assuming your score qualifies.

Why the stakes are worth it

The Erasmus Mundus scholarship covers tuition in full and pays a €1,400 monthly allowance plus travel and installation support — worth over €33,000 across a two-year programme. That is why the English requirement, unlike most admissions hurdles, is enforced to the letter: with ten to twenty applicants per funded place, consortia can afford to be strict. If your score is 6.0 and a favourite programme wants 6.5, remember most consortia assess applications holistically and some issue conditional offers — but a 6.5 sitting is often cheaper than a lost year.

Where to go next

If you are mapping applications across countries rather than programmes, our Europe without IELTS guide covers country-level rules, and the UK MOI guide explains how British universities treat the same letter differently.
